title: Teaspoon to Grams Converter — Spices, Salt, Sugar 2026
h1: Teaspoon to Grams Converter for Spices
description: Convert teaspoons to grams for salt, sugar, flour, spices & more. Real densities per ingredient: 1 tsp salt = 6g, sugar = 4g, pepper = 2g.
seoKeywords: how many grams in a teaspoon
intro:
A teaspoon is a fixed volume — about 5 mL — but its weight in grams changes dramatically depending on what's inside it. One teaspoon of fine table salt weighs 6 g, while the same spoon filled with dried oregano weighs only 1 g. That's a 6× difference from the same measuring tool.

This converter uses real bulk-density values for 20 common kitchen ingredients sourced from USDA FoodData Central. Select your ingredient, enter the number of flat teaspoons, and get the gram equivalent instantly — no guesswork, no generic '1 tsp = 5 g' approximation that's only accurate for water.

Useful when scaling recipes from US imperial (tsp, cups) to metric grams, when following a low-sodium diet with a salt-gram limit, or when a recipe asks for an unusual fraction of a teaspoon that's easier to weigh on a kitchen scale.
keyTakeaway: **Formula: Grams = teaspoons × grams-per-teaspoon (ingredient-specific)**. Key values: salt 6 g/tsp, sugar 4 g/tsp, flour 3 g/tsp, oregano 1 g/tsp, baking soda 4.8 g/tsp.
useCases: A bread recipe calls for 10 g of fine salt for 500 g of flour — the converter tells you that's exactly 1.67 teaspoons.
A low-sodium diet with a 5 g/day salt limit: find out how many teaspoons of each salt type that represents.
A US recipe says '2 tsp baking soda' — convert to 9.6 g for accurate scale measurement instead of trusting the spoon.
Halving a cake recipe that calls for 1 tsp baking powder: you need 0.5 tsp = 2 g, easy to weigh without fractions.

explanation:
## How it works

The formula is straightforward:

```
Grams = teaspoons × grams-per-teaspoon (ingredient-specific)
```

One flat teaspoon = **5 mL** of volume (metric and US culinary standard). The gram value depends on the **bulk density** of the specific ingredient — how much that 5 mL of volume actually weighs.

## Reference table (flat teaspoon = 5 mL)

| Ingredient | g/tsp | g/tbsp (×3) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fine table salt | 6.0 | 18.0 | Small crystals, high density |
| Coarse / sea salt | 4.5 | 13.5 | Large crystals, more air gaps |
| Flake salt (Maldon) | 2.8 | 8.4 | Voluminous thin flakes |
| White granulated sugar | 4.0 | 12.0 | Standard |
| Powdered / icing sugar | 3.0 | 9.0 | Finer, traps more air |
| Brown sugar | 4.5 | 13.5 | Moist, more compact |
| All-purpose flour | 3.0 | 9.0 | Unsifted, unpacked |
| Baking soda | 4.8 | 14.4 | Very fine, packs well |
| Baking powder | 4.0 | 12.0 | Baking soda + cream of tartar |
| Active dry yeast | 3.0 | 9.0 | Medium granules |
| Ground black pepper | 2.0 | 6.0 | Medium grind |
| Ground cinnamon | 2.6 | 7.8 | |
| Dried oregano | 1.0 | 3.0 | Leaf form, very light |
| Ground coffee | 2.0 | 6.0 | Medium grind |
| Cocoa powder | 2.6 | 7.8 | Unsweetened |
| Cornstarch | 2.5 | 7.5 | |
| Ground turmeric | 3.0 | 9.0 | |
| Ground cumin | 2.5 | 7.5 | |
| Paprika | 2.5 | 7.5 | |
| Chili flakes | 2.0 | 6.0 | |

## Common mistakes

- **Heaped vs flat teaspoon**: a heaped teaspoon weighs 1.5–2× a flat one. Culinary science uses **flat/leveled** unless stated otherwise.
- **Assuming 1 tsp = 5 g for everything**: that's only correct if the density is exactly 1 g/mL (like water). Salt is 6 g, oregano is 1 g.
- **Swapping baking soda and baking powder**: baking soda is ~3× more potent as a leavener — not a 1:1 substitute.
- **Different salt types**: fine table salt (6 g/tsp) vs coarse salt (4.5 g/tsp) — a 25% difference that matters in bread recipes.

faq.q: How many grams is 1 teaspoon of salt?
faq.a: 1 flat teaspoon of fine table salt = 6 g. This varies by salt type: coarse or sea salt = 4.5 g/tsp (larger crystals with more air gaps), and flake salt like Maldon = about 2.8 g/tsp (voluminous thin layers). This difference matters in bread baking — using coarse salt at the same teaspoon count as fine salt results in noticeably less salty bread.

faq.q: How many grams is 1 teaspoon of sugar?
faq.a: 1 flat teaspoon of white granulated sugar = 4 g. Powdered / icing sugar = 3 g/tsp (finer, more air trapped). Brown sugar = 4.5 g/tsp (moist and more compact). In caloric terms, 1 tsp of white sugar = 16 kcal. The WHO recommends fewer than 25 g of free sugars per day for adults — that's just 6 teaspoons.

faq.q: How many grams is 1 teaspoon of baking soda vs baking powder?
faq.a: Baking soda: 4.8 g per flat teaspoon. Baking powder: 4 g. These are not interchangeable: baking soda is approximately 3× more potent as a leavener. A recipe calling for '1 tsp baking soda' cannot be swapped for 1 tsp baking powder with the same result. The technical substitution is 1 tsp baking soda = 3 tsp baking powder.

faq.q: Why do spices like oregano weigh so little per teaspoon?
faq.a: Dried spices have a very low bulk density — most of the teaspoon volume is air between the particles or leaf fragments. Dried oregano weighs only 1 g/tsp, ground cinnamon 2.6 g/tsp, ground black pepper 2 g/tsp. Compare that to salt (6 g/tsp) or sugar (4 g/tsp). The active flavor compounds in spices are concentrated, so even 1 g of oregano packs significant flavor.

faq.q: What is 1 tablespoon in grams for common ingredients?
faq.a: 1 tablespoon = 3 teaspoons. So: fine salt = 18 g/tbsp, white sugar = 12 g/tbsp, all-purpose flour = 9 g/tbsp, baking soda = 14.4 g/tbsp, dried oregano = 3 g/tbsp. For liquids: olive oil ≈ 13.6 g/tbsp (density ~0.91 g/mL), honey ≈ 21 g/tbsp (density ~1.4 g/mL).

faq.q: Flat vs heaped teaspoon — how much does it matter?
faq.a: Flat (leveled) teaspoon: pass the straight edge of a knife across the top. This is the implicit standard in all written recipes unless otherwise specified. Heaped teaspoon: a mound on top, weighing 1.5–2× more depending on the ingredient. For salt: flat = 6 g, heaped ≈ 9–10 g. For sugar: flat = 4 g, heaped ≈ 6–7 g. In baking, using a heaped teaspoon of baking powder instead of flat can cause a cake to over-rise and then collapse.

faq.q: How accurate is this teaspoon to gram converter?
faq.a: The densities used are standard reference values from USDA FoodData Central, accurate within ±5–10% for typical home kitchen conditions. Real variation comes from: how tightly the ingredient is packed, humidity (moist brown sugar is denser), grind size (coarse vs fine pepper), and whether the spoon is leveled. For critical baking ratios, a kitchen scale is always more reliable than volume measures.

faq.q: Can I use this for measuring liquid ingredients?
faq.a: This converter is designed for dry/powdered ingredients. For liquids, 1 tsp = 5 mL by definition, and then you multiply by the liquid's density: water = 1 g/mL (5 g/tsp), olive oil ≈ 0.91 g/mL (4.5 g/tsp), honey ≈ 1.4 g/mL (7 g/tsp). Liquids generally measure well in teaspoons without needing density correction, since they self-level in the spoon.

faq.q: What's the difference between US teaspoon and UK teaspoon in grams?
faq.a: US teaspoon: 4.93 mL — the difference from 5 mL is less than 2%, negligible for cooking. UK teaspoon: 5.9 mL — 18% larger than the US/metric teaspoon. For potent spices or leaveners, this can matter: 1 UK tsp of baking soda = about 7.1 g vs 4.8 g for the metric version. Always check which system a recipe originates from.

faq.q: Is it worth buying a kitchen scale instead of using teaspoons?
faq.a: For baking, bread making, and fermentation: yes, absolutely. A digital kitchen scale eliminates all density, packing, and volume-system errors. For everyday cooking — a stew, a dressing, a sauce — well-used teaspoons are entirely sufficient. The practical middle ground: if you bake occasionally, a basic 1 g-precision scale (under $20) already meaningfully improves results, especially for leaveners, salt, and yeast.
